cues.text: Forty Hours in Holy Week
At Eastertide 1570, the church of St. Erasmus in Veroli, Italy, was observing the Forty Hours' devotion.

This involved continuous adoration of the Blessed Sacrament exposed before the faithful, following the custom by which each of the town's lay confraternities took turns keeping an hour of prayer before the altar.
Signs in the Host
On the Tuesday following Easter, during the exposition, witnesses reported seeing luminous figures appear within the consecrated Host itself.
Tradition holds specifically that the Christ Child was seen amid the radiance, in the posture of blessing, surrounded by what some accounts describe as small attending figures like adoring angels.
One witness's own recorded testimony describes seeing 'a most brilliant star' at the base of the chalice, with the Host resting above it.
A Growing Crowd
As word spread through Veroli, the church filled with residents hurrying from across the town to see the phenomenon for themselves.
The appearances reportedly continued before the growing crowd for some time, before ecclesiastical authorities began formally gathering testimony from those present.
A Long Preservation
The Host at the center of the event was preserved and venerated for an unusually long span — some 112 years — before finally being consumed according to custom.
The chalice, paten, and silver case used in the original exposition have all been kept ever since among the church's reliquaries.
The chalice is still brought out once a year for Mass on the Tuesday after Easter, in direct continuity with the original event.
Legacy
Veroli marked the event’s fourth centenary in 1970 with a diocesan Eucharistic Congress.
The church continues a monthly First Friday adoration in its honor, closing the town’s other churches for the hour.
The community can thus gather at the church where the sign was first reported.
The Veroli account belongs to a smaller category of Eucharistic tradition centered on visions witnessed during formal adoration.
It concerns neither theft, transformation, nor crisis—a sign, in the telling, given simply to those who had already set the hours aside to watch.
